title: Procrastination Tops Academic Struggles, Study Finds
paragraphs: Students face many challenges that can affect their studies, from stress and anxiety to money problems. But according to a large new study, the issue that harms students' academic performance most often is something far more ordinary: procrastination.

The study was carried out by Itamar Shatz, an affiliated lecturer at the University of Cambridge, and published in October in the journal PLOS One. It analyzed survey data from 65,950 students at 97 colleges and universities in the United States. Procrastination was compared with 35 other life and health issues, including stress, anxiety, depression, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and financial difficulties.

When students were asked whether they had experienced different problems in the past year, procrastination was the second most common issue, reported by 72.3% of students. Only stress was more common, at 73.8%. Anxiety came third, at 65%.

However, the most striking finding concerned the impact on academic performance. When students were asked which problems had harmed their studies, procrastination came out clearly on top, mentioned by 45.4% of students. That was 1.5 times as many as anxiety, the second most common answer, and more than twice as many as depression. Among students who were affected by each problem, only ADHD was more harmful to their academic work.
Undergraduate students were more likely to struggle with procrastination than postgraduates, at 74.8% compared with 66.2%.
The study also described a harmful cycle. Procrastination causes stress, stress disrupts sleep, and poor sleep in turn leads to more procrastination.

Shatz described the level of impact as "pretty staggering." Importantly, Shatz argued that problems with time management are a symptom of procrastination, not its cause. This means that simply teaching students time management skills may not be enough to solve the problem.

Instead, Shatz offered several recommendations for educators. These include breaking large tasks into smaller, more manageable parts, setting smaller and more frequent deadlines, and reassuring students that it is acceptable to make mistakes. Shatz also advised avoiding overly harsh criticism, which can make students feel ashamed, and balancing accountability with compassion.
